name: Northern Europe & Arctic
tagline: Fjords, wilderness, and the midnight sun
intro: Northern Europe and the Arctic represent the furthest reach of the superyacht charter world — and for those who seek them out, some of the most extraordinary cruising available.

This is expedition territory. The season runs from June to August, the conditions are variable, and the fleet is specialist. The reward is something entirely different from the Mediterranean and Caribbean: scale, silence, and a level of remoteness that is increasingly rare.

Norway is the natural entry point. The fjords — Hardangerfjord, Sognefjord, Geirangerfjord — are among the most dramatic landscapes in Europe. Waterfalls drop directly into calm, dark water, and mountains rise vertically from the sea. In midsummer, the midnight sun extends daylight well into the night, giving each anchorage a distinctive atmosphere.

Scotland offers a different kind of wildness — the Hebrides, the West Coast and the Caledonian Canal. Whisky distilleries, ancient castles, seabird colonies and weather that forms part of the experience. St Kilda, forty miles beyond the Outer Hebrides, rewards those who make the passage.

Greenland is the furthest expression of this region — icebergs, vast fjords and near-total wilderness. A small number of specialist expedition yachts operate here. For those who do, the experience is difficult to replicate elsewhere.

locations.name: Norway & the Fjords
locations.tagline: Geirangerfjord, Sognefjord, the midnight sun. The most dramatic coastal scenery in Europe
description: Norway is where most Northern Europe charters begin — and for many, where the concept of expedition sailing becomes real for the first time.

Bergen is the natural gateway. The UNESCO-listed Bryggen wharf, the fish market and the surrounding mountains make it one of the most distinctive port cities in Europe. From here, the fjords open in every direction.

Hardangerfjord is the most approachable — softer in character, lined with orchards and punctuated by waterfalls that drop directly to the water. Sognefjord is the longest and deepest fjord in Norway, its innermost arms extending far into the mountains, with Flåm at the end of one of the most dramatic valley passages in Scandinavia. Geirangerfjord is the headline — steep cliff walls, the Seven Sisters waterfall cascading in parallel streams, and a scale that requires time to absorb. UNESCO listed, and deservedly so.

The Lofoten Islands, further north, are in a different register entirely. Jagged peaks rise directly from the sea, traditional red fishing villages cling to rocky outcrops, and the light — particularly in the long evenings of midsummer — is unlike anywhere else in Europe.
Norwegian infrastructure is excellent throughout. The experience is remote by character, not by logistics.
whyCharter: Geirangerfjord — UNESCO World Heritage fjord, one of the most dramatic in Europe
Seven Sisters waterfall — one of Norway's most recognised natural landmarks
Lofoten Islands — jagged peaks, red villages, exceptional midsummer light
Midnight sun — continuous daylight in June and July
Bergen — one of Europe's most distinctive port cities
Strong marina infrastructure — remote by character, not by logistics

locations.name: Scotland
locations.tagline: The Hebrides, the West Coast and St Kilda. Wild, historic and entirely its own
description: Scotland is not a charter destination for those seeking guaranteed sunshine. It is a destination for those drawn to something more genuine — wild coastlines, layered history, extraordinary wildlife and sailing that asks something of you in return.

The West Coast and the Hebrides form the heart of Scottish charter. Oban is the natural base — well connected, well equipped and the gateway to an archipelago of over 900 islands. The Sound of Mull, Tobermory's painted houses, Fingal's Cave on Staffa, and Skye's Cuillin mountains rising above the anchorage at Portree — the west coast delivers something distinctive on every passage.

Islay, the southernmost of the Inner Hebrides, is home to some of the world's most respected whisky distilleries — Laphroaig, Ardbeg, Bowmore — several of which sit directly on the waterfront and can be reached by tender.

The Outer Hebrides — Lewis and Harris — extend the cruising ground into genuinely remote waters. St Kilda, forty miles beyond, rewards those who wait for the right weather window. A UNESCO dual World Heritage site, it is unlike anywhere else in the British Isles.
Orkney and Shetland, at the northern extreme, offer Norse heritage, dramatic cliff scenery and wildlife that includes puffins, orcas and seals.
whyCharter: St Kilda — UNESCO dual World Heritage site, unlike anywhere else in the British Isles
Islay whisky distilleries — Laphroaig, Ardbeg, Bowmore — accessible by tender
West Coast and Hebrides — over 900 islands, wild and largely untouched
Fingal's Cave — one of Europe's most distinctive natural formations
Orkney and Shetland — Norse heritage, puffins, orcas
Genuine remoteness within reach of the UK mainland

locations.name: Greenland
locations.tagline: Icebergs, vast fjords, near-total wilderness. Expedition sailing at its most elemental
description: Greenland is not a charter destination in the conventional sense. There are no marinas, no beach clubs, no established itineraries. There is ice, silence, scale, and a landscape so indifferent to human presence that the experience of moving through it leaves a lasting impression.

A very small number of expedition yachts operate in Greenlandic waters — ice-strengthened, properly equipped, and crewed by people who understand what is required. For those aboard, the experience is unlike anything the established charter world can offer.

Disko Bay and the Ilulissat Icefjord form the most accessible entry point. The fjord, a UNESCO World Heritage site, produces some of the largest icebergs in the northern hemisphere — vast, silent structures drifting at a pace that alters your sense of time. The light in July and August, with the midnight sun still present, gives the ice a quality that is difficult to capture.
Prince Christian Sound, at the southern tip, is one of the great fjord passages in the world — a narrow channel flanked by glaciers and near-vertical rock faces, largely inaccessible except by sea.
The season is July and August. Ice conditions shape the itinerary more than any plan — and that is part of its appeal.
whyCharter: Ilulissat Icefjord — UNESCO World Heritage site, icebergs on an exceptional scale
Prince Christian Sound — one of the great fjord passages in the world
Midnight sun — continuous light throughout July and August
Near-total wilderness — one of the least visited coastlines globally
Expedition sailing at its most elemental — a different category entirely
For clients who have explored widely and are looking for something further

name: Western Mediterranean
tagline: Riviera glamour, Tyrrhenian shores, Balearic blues
intro: The Western Mediterranean is where superyacht charter began, and it remains one of the most established charter regions in the world. From the Côte d'Azur to the Balearic Islands, from the southern tip of Corsica to the coastline of Sicily, this is a region of extraordinary range — in landscape, culture and overall experience.

The infrastructure here is unmatched anywhere in the world. Antibes is the largest superyacht base on earth. Palma de Mallorca, Cannes, Monaco, Olbia and Naples together cover the full sweep of the region, with world-class marinas, exceptional provisioning, and a depth of technical support that allows captains and crew to plan ambitious itineraries with confidence. The season runs from May to October, with July and August bringing the full theatre of the Mediterranean summer.

But the Western Mediterranean is not only defined by the well-known names. Corsica's southern anchorages, the Lavezzi Islands, the quieter corners of Sardinia's La Maddalena archipelago, and the smaller Balearic islands of Formentera and Menorca — these are the places that define the region. The area rewards both the first-time charterer and the client who has been returning for decades and still finds something new.
Four countries, four distinct characters — each offering a different expression of the Mediterranean.

locations.name: France
locations.tagline: The Riviera, Saint-Tropez, Corsica. Effortlessly the standard
description: France moves between two entirely different expressions of the Mediterranean — and does both with a clarity few destinations can match.

The Côte d'Azur is the season. Saint-Tropez at anchor off Pampelonne, a tender ashore to Club 55, an evening in the old port — this is what people mean when they talk about the Riviera. The Cannes Film Festival, the Monaco Grand Prix and the Cannes Yachting Festival define the calendar. Belle époque facades, casino terraces and Michelin-starred tables sit steps from the dock. Unapologetic, unhurried, and entirely itself.

Corsica is the counterpoint. Six hours offshore, the tone changes completely — maquis-scented hillsides, limestone cliffs dropping into clear water, and anchorages that feel genuinely remote even in August. Bonifacio and the Lavezzi Islands are among the finest cruising grounds in the Mediterranean. Saint-Florent and Calvi offer a quieter rhythm, with strong restaurants and easy provisioning.
The Riviera defines the season. Corsica is where you step away from it.
whyCharter: World-class marinas and superyacht infrastructure
Iconic beaches — Pampelonne, Porquerolles, Lavezzi Islands
Established social and events calendar
Exceptional dining — from beach clubs to Michelin-starred tables
Fashion, art and cultural depth
Access to Corsica's more remote anchorages

locations.name: Monaco
locations.tagline: Small in scale. Singular in influence
description: Monaco does not need context. Port Hercule is one of the most recognised harbours on earth, Monte Carlo one of the most storied addresses. The principality is small by every geographical measure and outsized in every other — in ambition, atmosphere and the density of exceptional experiences available within walking distance of the dock.

Yachts base here, particularly for the Monaco Grand Prix, when the harbour transforms into the most electric setting on the Riviera calendar. Outside of race weekend, Monaco rewards those who look beyond the obvious. The Casino de Monte-Carlo, long associated with James Bond and still drawing an international crowd each evening. The grand hotels — Hôtel de Paris, the Hermitage, the Monte-Carlo Beach — each operating at a standard few cities in the world can match. Jimmy'z and Twiga draw an international crowd throughout the summer season, with world-class DJs and a clientele that reflects Monaco's singular position. And Fontvieille, the quieter quarter below the palace rock, for those who want to step away from the theatre of the port.
Everything here is condensed. Nothing is diluted.
whyCharter: The Monaco Grand Prix — the defining event charter experience
Casino de Monte-Carlo — one of the most recognisable gaming rooms in the world
Grand hotels — Hôtel de Paris, Hermitage, Monte-Carlo Beach
Jimmy'z and Twiga — established nightlife, international crowd
Exceptional fine dining and private members' culture
Year-round destination — no defined off-season

locations.name: Italy
locations.tagline: Four distinct cruising grounds. Each one a different Italy
description: Italy's charter grounds are among the most varied in the Mediterranean — and unlike most regions, each territory is a self-contained itinerary. Most clients choose one.

sections.heading: The Italian Riviera
sections.body: Runs from the French border through Portofino and Santa Margherita along the Ligurian coast — refined, unhurried, and well suited to shorter charters. Portofino in particular remains one of the most beautiful small harbours in Europe.

sections.heading: The Amalfi Coast
sections.body: Based out of Naples. From here, Capri, Positano, Procida and the dramatic cliff towns of the Amalfi coastline are all within easy reach — a compact cruising ground of extraordinary beauty and cultural depth.

sections.heading: Sardinia
sections.body: Sardinia means the Costa Smeralda. Porto Cervo, the La Maddalena archipelago and the wild Bonifacio Strait offer a combination of world-class marina infrastructure and genuinely remote anchorages — often in the same day.

sections.heading: Sicily & the Aeolian Islands
sections.body: Demand more time — a ten-day minimum to do the passage justice. Stromboli, Lipari and Panarea are the stepping stones south, with Sicily itself offering ancient cities, baroque architecture and water that turns every shade of blue.

whyCharter: Four distinct territories — each a different experience
Portofino — one of Europe's finest small harbours
Amalfi Coast — dramatic scenery, cultural depth, Capri
Costa Smeralda — world-class marina and remote wilderness
Sicily — ancient history, baroque cities, extraordinary water
Aeolian Islands — volcanic, raw and largely unspoiled

locations.name: Spain
locations.tagline: The Balearic Islands. Home waters
description: The Balearic Islands are the heart of Western Mediterranean charter — and for Sinclair Yachting, home waters.

sections.heading: Mallorca
sections.body: The most varied of the four. The northwest coast rises into the Serra de Tramuntana — a UNESCO mountain range dropping dramatically to the sea, with coves accessible only by boat. To the south, the protected waters around Cabrera offer some of the finest anchorages in the archipelago. Ashore, the island moves between Michelin-starred tables in Palma's old town and unhurried chiringuitos that explain why people keep returning.

sections.heading: Menorca
sections.body: Quieter to the north — a UNESCO biosphere reserve with natural anchorages, clear water and a pace the other islands have long since left behind.

sections.heading: Ibiza
sections.body: Needs no introduction. Beach clubs, open-air venues and an energy that runs from noon to dawn — balanced by some of the most beautiful anchorages in the Mediterranean. Es Vedrà at sunset remains one of the great charter experiences.

sections.heading: Formentera
sections.body: Reached by tender — shallow, translucent water, minimal development and a complete shift in pace.

locations.footer: Barcelona operates as an occasional static or event charter base — well positioned, but not a primary cruising ground at this level.
whyCharter: Four islands, four distinct cruising experiences
Cabrera — protected national park, exceptional anchorages
Serra de Tramuntana — UNESCO coastline, dramatic and largely sea-accessed
Ibiza — beach clubs, nightlife and hidden coves
Formentera — exceptional shallow-water cruising
Outstanding food — Michelin-starred dining to relaxed chiringuitos

name: Eastern Mediterranean
tagline: Ancient coastlines, crystalline water, island light
intro: The Eastern Mediterranean is where the sea takes on a different character. The light is sharper, more golden, and the coastlines carry a depth of history that the western basin cannot match. From the Ionian Islands to the Turquoise Coast, from the Dalmatian archipelago to the Dodecanese, this is a region that rewards those who take the time to explore properly.

The infrastructure has matured significantly. Athens, Dubrovnik, Bodrum and Split are all established charter bases with strong technical support and provisioning. The season runs from May to October, with the Aegean at its best in June and September, when the meltemi eases and anchorages are quieter.

But the Eastern Mediterranean is defined by what lies beyond the marinas. Remote island anchorages, ancient cities approached from the water, and landscapes that have changed little in centuries. Croatia's Dalmatian islands, the volcanic Cyclades, the pine-scented bays of the Turkish coast — these are the places that stay with you.
Three distinct territories, each offering a different expression of the Eastern Mediterranean.

locations.name: Greece
locations.tagline: The Ionian, the Aegean, the Dodecanese. Ancient, luminous, inexhaustible
description: Greece is one of the most varied and rewarding charter destinations in the Eastern Mediterranean — and one that benefits from a considered approach.

Athens serves as the primary starting point for most charters. The Saronic Gulf — Hydra, Spetses, Poros — is particularly well suited to shorter itineraries, with immediate access to the islands. The Cyclades are accessible within a standard week, though the southern islands, including Santorini, are best explored over a longer itinerary.

The Ionian Islands — Corfu, Kefalonia, Lefkada, Zakynthos — sit on the western coast, greener and calmer than the Aegean, with a more sheltered style of cruising. The region can be explored independently or incorporated into a wider itinerary.

Further east, the Dodecanese — Rhodes, Patmos, Symi, Kos — offer a more expansive and largely uncrowded cruising ground, close to the Turkish coast. For those who venture here, it is among the most rewarding sailing in the Mediterranean.
The meltemi shapes the Aegean through July and August, while June and September offer particularly favourable conditions.
whyCharter: The Saronic Gulf — accessible, well suited to shorter charters
Cyclades — Mykonos, Paros, Milos, Santorini — iconic and varied
Ionian Islands — calmer waters, greener landscape, consistent sailing
Dodecanese — historic, remote and largely uncrowded
The Corinth Canal — one of the defining passages in Mediterranean sailing
Ancient history present at every stage of the itinerary

locations.name: Croatia & Montenegro
locations.tagline: The Dalmatian coast, a thousand islands, and Kotor Bay
description: Croatia has become one of the most compelling charter destinations in the Mediterranean — and one of the fastest rising. The Dalmatian coast offers a combination of medieval walled cities, crystal-clear Adriatic water and an archipelago of over a thousand islands that rewards exploration in a way few coastlines can match.

Dubrovnik is the natural anchor — one of the most beautiful cities in Europe, and extraordinary when approached by sea. Hvar has evolved into a genuinely high-end destination, with restaurants, beach clubs and energy to stand alongside the best of the Riviera. Korčula and Brač offer a quieter, more unhurried character, while the Kornati Islands — a national park of bare limestone and translucent water — are among the most dramatic sailing grounds in the Mediterranean. Split operates as the primary charter base, well connected and well equipped.

Montenegro sits at the southern end of the cruising ground and deserves consideration in its own right. Kotor Bay — a fjord-like inlet ringed by medieval fortifications and mountain walls — is one of the most striking anchorages in Europe. The country's favourable tax environment also makes it an attractive base for certain charter arrangements. A conversation worth having with your broker.
whyCharter: Over a thousand islands — one of the great sailing archipelagos
Dubrovnik — medieval walled city, extraordinary from the sea
Hvar — high-end destination competing with the best of the Riviera
Kornati Islands — national park, raw and dramatic
Kotor Bay — one of the most striking anchorages in Europe
Favourable tax environment in Montenegro

locations.name: Turkey
locations.tagline: The Turquoise Coast. Bodrum, Göcek and the bays that remain largely undiscovered
description: Turkey is one of the most beautiful and least understood charter destinations in the Mediterranean. The Turquoise Coast is verdant, sheltered and distinctive — pine forests running to the water's edge, bays accessible only by sea, and a style of hospitality that feels entirely its own.

The Gulf of Fethiye is the centre of it. The Pine Islands, the Blue Lagoon at Ölüdeniz, and the anchorages scattered across the gulf offer some of the most relaxed cruising in the Mediterranean. The water is clear, the bays are protected, and the quality of light — particularly in the early morning and late evening — is exceptional.

Bodrum is the primary charter base — cosmopolitan, well equipped and well connected — with access to both the peninsula and the wider Aegean coast. Göcek, further south, is quieter and more contained, often preferred for its immediate access to the Pine Islands and the gulf.
Marmaris extends the cruising ground south and west, opening access to the Bozburun Peninsula — a largely unspoiled coastline of small harbours and quiet anchorages.
The cuisine throughout is a defining feature. Turkish hospitality, aboard and ashore, sets a standard few regions match.
whyCharter: Gulf of Fethiye — Pine Islands, protected bays, exceptional cruising conditions
Verdant coastline — greener and more sheltered than much of the Aegean
Turkish cuisine and hospitality — consistently outstanding
Largely unspoiled anchorages — fewer crowds than the Western Mediterranean
Bodrum — established charter base with strong infrastructure
Bozburun Peninsula — quiet, traditional and lightly developed

name: Caribbean & Bahamas
tagline: Trade winds, turquoise water, and the other great charter season
intro: The Caribbean and the Bahamas represent the second chapter of the superyacht charter calendar — running from November through to May, when the Mediterranean is out of season, and offering a breadth of experience that rivals anything the Med can provide.

The region divides into distinct territories, each with its own character, infrastructure and licensing jurisdiction. The British Virgin Islands and US Virgin Islands sit side by side but operate as separate charter grounds. St Martin is the gateway to St Barths and the Leeward Islands. Antigua anchors the sailing heritage of the eastern Caribbean. The Grenadines offer some of the most unspoiled cruising in the region.

The Bahamas is distinct — and uniquely, open year-round. Positioned off the Florida coast, with a longer operating season than much of the Caribbean, it is defined by shallow turquoise water, deserted cays and a style of cruising entirely its own. The fleet typically operates from Nassau, with Fort Lauderdale and Miami serving as key access points.

The trade winds blow consistently from the east, the water is warm and clear, and the pace of life aboard is unlike anything in the Mediterranean. For clients who charter in the Med during summer, the Caribbean is the natural winter extension — same fleet, same standard, an entirely different setting.
Six territories. Each one worth a season in its own right.

seasonConditions.hurricaneSeason: June – November (Caribbean islands — Bahamas less affected but still seasonal)
seasonConditions.charterBases: Tortola · St Thomas · St Martin · Antigua · Grenada · Nassau · Fort Lauderdale

locations.name: British Virgin Islands
locations.tagline: The classic Caribbean charter ground. Protected waters, consistent trade winds, exceptional sailing
description: The British Virgin Islands are where many clients begin their Caribbean charter experience — and where many return, season after season, for good reason.

The Sir Francis Drake Channel is one of the finest protected sailing passages in the world. Consistent trade winds, short distances between islands, and an infrastructure built around charter for decades — the BVI delivers the classic Caribbean sailing experience with a reliability few territories can match.

Tortola is the principal base. Road Town provides the core charter infrastructure — well equipped, well connected, and the natural starting point for most itineraries. From here, the islands open up in every direction.

Virgin Gorda is often the first stop — The Baths, the extraordinary granite boulder formations at the southern tip, and the calmer waters of North Sound to the north. Jost Van Dyke is the social centre of the BVI — White Bay, the Soggy Dollar Bar, and afternoons that extend into the evening. Norman Island, often associated with Treasure Island, offers excellent snorkelling at The Caves and one of the more atmospheric anchorages in the Caribbean.
The BVI is compact, varied and consistent — equally suited to first-time charterers and returning clients.
whyCharter: Sir Francis Drake Channel — one of the world's great protected sailing passages
The Baths — distinctive granite formations unique to Virgin Gorda
Jost Van Dyke — the social centre of the BVI
Established charter infrastructure — developed specifically for sailing itineraries
Compact cruising ground — multiple islands within short reach
Well suited to both first-time and experienced charterers

locations.name: US Virgin Islands
locations.tagline: St Thomas, St John and the American gateway to the Caribbean
description: The US Virgin Islands are the American gateway to the Caribbean — and for many US clients, the natural starting point for a first charter.

St Thomas is the base. Charlotte Amalie is one of the most well-connected ports in the Caribbean — strong infrastructure, direct access from the US mainland, and a harbour that opens onto sailing grounds far quieter than the port itself suggests.

St John, a short passage east, is the reason many clients choose the USVI. Two thirds of the island is US National Park — protected, largely undeveloped, and exceptionally beautiful. Trunk Bay is one of the most recognised beaches in the Caribbean, and the anchorages along the north shore are consistently outstanding.

St Croix lies forty miles to the south — quieter and less visited, with Buck Island's protected reef offering excellent snorkelling and Christiansted's Danish colonial architecture adding a different dimension ashore.

The USVI requires no passport for US citizens and operates in US dollars — practical advantages that matter when planning a first Caribbean charter. The British Virgin Islands lie immediately to the east but operate as a separate charter jurisdiction — a conversation worth having with your broker.
whyCharter: St John — US National Park, Trunk Bay, outstanding north shore anchorages
No passport required for US citizens — seamless access from the mainland
St Thomas — well connected, strong charter infrastructure
St Croix — Buck Island reef, colonial architecture, less visited
US dollars throughout — familiar and straightforward
Natural stepping stone into the broader Caribbean

locations.name: St Barths, St Martin & the Leeward Islands
locations.tagline: The energy of St Barths, the base of St Martin, and the islands between
description: St Martin sits at the centre of the Leeward Islands charter circuit — a well-connected base from which some of the most varied and rewarding sailing in the Caribbean unfolds within a short passage.

The island divides between the French north — Marigot, Grand Case, quiet lagoon anchorages — and the Dutch south, Sint Maarten, which provides the marina infrastructure, provisioning and nightlife. Between them, they service the charter fleet effectively.

St Barths is the headline destination. Twenty miles to the southeast, Gustavia is one of the most refined small harbours in the world — expensive, beautiful and worth the journey. The anchorage, the restaurants, the boutiques, and the sense of being at the centre of Caribbean high season — St Barths delivers it all.
Anguilla lies five miles to the north — low-key and unhurried, with some of the finest beaches in the Caribbean and a restaurant scene that far exceeds its size.
Saba, to the southwest, is volcanic, dramatic and largely undeveloped — a world-class diving destination for those looking to step away from the social circuit.
St Kitts and Nevis extend the itinerary further south — lush, historic and less frequented than the islands to the north.
whyCharter: St Barths — Gustavia harbour, world-class restaurants, Caribbean at its most refined
Anguilla — pristine beaches, outstanding food, relaxed luxury
Saba — dramatic volcanic island, world-class diving
St Martin — strong charter infrastructure across both sides of the island
St Kitts & Nevis — lush, historic and less visited
Six islands within easy reach of a single base

locations.name: Antigua & Barbuda
locations.tagline: English Harbour, Sailing Week, and one of the region's defining charter bases
description: Antigua is one of the Caribbean's most established charter bases — and one that rewards those who take the time to explore it properly.

English Harbour and Falmouth Harbour sit side by side on the southern coast — two of the most historically significant and best-equipped anchorages in the region. Nelson's Dockyard, a UNESCO World Heritage site, gives the harbour a depth of character that few Caribbean bases can match. Antigua Sailing Week, held each April, draws an international racing fleet and remains one of the defining events on the Caribbean calendar.

The island offers remarkable variety — consistent trade winds, over 365 beaches, and anchorages that range from the social atmosphere of the harbours to the quieter bays along the north and west coasts.

Barbuda lies thirty miles to the north — largely undeveloped, exceptionally quiet, with pink sand beaches and one of the largest frigate bird colonies in the world. It is among the least visited and most distinctive islands in the Caribbean.

For those with more time, Antigua provides a natural starting point for a southbound passage through the Windward Islands — Guadeloupe, Dominica, Martinique and St Lucia — one of the great extended itineraries in Caribbean sailing.
whyCharter: Nelson's Dockyard — UNESCO World Heritage site and a defining Caribbean anchorage
Antigua Sailing Week — one of the region's premier sailing events
Barbuda — pink sand beaches, frigate bird sanctuary, largely undeveloped
Over 365 beaches — exceptional variety for a single island
Gateway to the Windward Islands for extended itineraries
Consistent trade winds and strong sailing conditions

locations.name: St Lucia, St Vincent & The Grenadines
locations.tagline: The unspoiled Caribbean. Islands that have retained their original pace
description: For those who have chartered the Caribbean widely, the Grenadines tend to become the answer. This is the region at its most elemental — unspoiled islands, exceptional water, and a pace that more developed territories have long since left behind.

St Lucia is the natural starting point from the north. The twin volcanic Pitons rising from the sea at Soufrière create one of the defining arrival moments in Caribbean sailing. Marigot Bay, Rodney Bay and the island's lush interior make St Lucia one of the most visually striking destinations in the region.

From St Vincent southward, the chain begins to open up. Bequia is the first stop — relaxed, unhurried, with a genuine sailing community and restaurants that reward the short passage. Mustique offers something entirely different — private, discreet, and deliberately removed.
Further south, the Tobago Cays Marine Park is the anchorage that stays with people longest. Uninhabited islands, protected reef, turtles and water of exceptional clarity — accessible only by sea.
Palm Island, Petit St Vincent and Carriacou extend the itinerary toward Grenada, each adding depth to what is, for many, the most rewarding cruising ground in the Caribbean.
whyCharter: Tobago Cays — protected marine park, turtles, uninhabited islands, exceptional water
St Lucia — the Pitons, Marigot Bay, one of the Caribbean's most striking landscapes
Mustique — private, discreet, highly curated
Bequia — authentic character with a strong sailing community
Unspoiled throughout — fewer crowds than most Caribbean territories
For many, the most rewarding cruising ground in the region

locations.name: The Bahamas
locations.tagline: Shallow water, deserted cays, extraordinary light. A different kind of charter entirely
description: The Bahamas is a different kind of charter — and that is precisely its appeal.

The water is shallow, warm and exceptionally clear. Sandbars emerge from the sea, colour shifts from deep blue to pale turquoise within metres, and the light is unlike anywhere else in the Caribbean. One of the most visually distinctive cruising grounds in the world.

The Exuma Cays are the centre of it. The Exuma Cays Land and Sea Park offers pristine reef and exceptional clarity. Big Major Cay — where wild pigs swim out to meet passing yachts — is one of the most recognised locations in the Bahamas. Allen's Cay's iguanas and the blue holes throughout the chain add to a cruising ground that rewards exploration.
The shallow nature of the Exumas means deeper-draft vessels rely on tenders for many anchorages. Explorer yachts and shallower motor yachts are particularly well suited.

Nassau is the primary gateway, with Fort Lauderdale and Miami as key US access points. The Abacos offer a more sailing-oriented cruising ground — the Sea of Abaco and Hope Town's lighthouse among the highlights.
Open year-round, the Bahamas operates on a different seasonal pattern to much of the Caribbean.
whyCharter: Exuma Cays — Land and Sea Park, exceptional reef, outstanding water clarity
Big Major Cay — swimming pigs, one of the region's most distinctive experiences
Shallow turquoise water unlike anywhere else in the Caribbean
Year-round cruising, with a longer operating window than many island groups
Harbour Island — pink sand beach, one of the most recognised in the region
Well positioned for US clients — Fort Lauderdale and Miami access

name: Central & South America
tagline: Wild coasts, ancient cultures, and some of the least chartered waters in the world
intro: Central and South America represent some of the most diverse and least chartered waters globally — a region where the gap between what exists and what most clients have experienced remains significant.

The Pacific and Caribbean coasts of Central America, the island archipelagos of Panama, the colonial ports of Colombia, the wildlife-led itineraries of the Galapagos, and the more remote waters of Brazil all contribute to a charter landscape that is broad, varied, and still developing. Infrastructure is more limited than in the Mediterranean or Caribbean, but sufficient for those planning with the right expertise.

Panama is the natural entry point. The San Blas Islands — Kuna Yala — are one of the more distinctive cruising grounds in the Americas: hundreds of low-lying islands, clear water and an indigenous culture that continues to define the region. The Panama Canal itself remains a passage of particular interest.

Colombia, Costa Rica, the Galapagos and Brazil each offer a different experience. This is not a region for the familiar — it is for clients who have chartered widely and are looking for something less conventional.
The season broadly aligns with the Caribbean — November to April — though individual territories vary.

seasonConditions.charterBases: Panama City · Cartagena · Puerto Caldera · Puerto Ayora

locations.name: Panama & the San Blas Islands
locations.tagline: Kuna Yala, the Panama Canal, and one of the more distinctive cruising grounds in the Americas
description: Panama offers two entirely different charter experiences — and sits alongside one of the most significant engineering projects in the world.

The San Blas Islands — Kuna Yala — are the Caribbean coast at its most elemental. Three hundred and sixty-five low-lying coral islands stretch along the shoreline, governed and protected by the Kuna people, who have maintained sovereignty here for generations. There is no outside development, no hotel infrastructure, no road access. The only way to experience it properly is by sea. The water is shallow, clear and notably unspoiled — one of the more distinctive cruising grounds in the Americas.
Bocas del Toro, to the west, offers a different character — mangrove channels, surf breaks, and accessible infrastructure while retaining strong natural appeal.

The Panama Canal — connecting the Caribbean to the Pacific across 83 kilometres of engineered waterway — defines Panama's place in maritime history. It is not a charter itinerary, but its presence shapes the country and makes Panama a natural base for yachts repositioning between oceans.
The Pacific coast opens access to the Pearl Islands and the Gulf of Panama — less visited, with seasonal diving and whale activity.
whyCharter: San Blas Islands — no development, no road access, experienced primarily by sea
Kuna Yala — indigenous governance and a culturally distinct cruising ground
Bocas del Toro — accessible nature, mangroves and surf
Pearl Islands — seasonal diving and whale activity
Panama Canal — a defining feature of global maritime routes
Two distinct coastlines within a single charter destination

locations.name: Colombia
locations.tagline: Cartagena — one of the most established colonial ports in the Americas, approached from the sea
description: Cartagena is one of the most established colonial cities in the Americas — and one that is best approached from the water.

The walled old city, a UNESCO World Heritage site, rises above the waterfront in a palette of ochre, terracotta and deep blue, with the Castillo San Felipe set above the skyline. The streets within the walls are among the most atmospheric in South America: balconies, shaded plazas, and restaurants that open into the evening. The city rewards time ashore, and arrival by yacht offers a considered introduction.
Thirty minutes offshore, the Rosario Islands provide a clear contrast — twenty-seven islands of shallow water, coral reef and near-total quiet, accessible within a single day.

Further east, Santa Marta and Tayrona National Park extend the cruising ground along one of the more dramatic coastlines in the region. Jungle meets the sea, the beaches remain largely undeveloped, and the park protects a stretch of coastline that still sees relatively limited access.
Colombia's reputation has shifted significantly. Cartagena in particular is now a sophisticated and welcoming destination — culturally rich and deserving of more time than most itineraries allow.
whyCharter: Cartagena — UNESCO World Heritage walled city, best approached from the sea
Rosario Islands — coral reefs, clear water, within easy reach
Tayrona National Park — jungle coastline, largely undeveloped
Strong cultural identity — architecture, food and music
Growing charter infrastructure in Cartagena
A destination that rewards extended itineraries

locations.name: Costa Rica & the Pacific
locations.tagline: The Gulf of Papagayo and a coastline defined by wildlife and seasonality
description: Costa Rica is defined as much by what surrounds the water as what lies within it — a coastline of exceptional biodiversity where jungle, wildlife and sea exist in close proximity.

The Gulf of Papagayo on the Pacific northwest coast is the primary charter base — a protected bay with established marina infrastructure and reliable conditions during the dry season from December to April. The Nicoya Peninsula extends south along a more dramatic and less visited stretch of coastline, with surf breaks and anchorages that reward exploration.

Offshore, Cocos Island lies over 500 kilometres into the Pacific — one of the most remote and biodiverse marine environments in the region. A UNESCO World Heritage site, accessible only by specialist expedition vessel and known for hammerhead sharks, whale sharks and manta rays. Not a conventional charter itinerary, but for the right client and vessel, it is a notable extension.
Along the coast, humpback whales migrate through Pacific waters between December and April. Sea turtles nest on protected beaches, and birdlife and forest wildlife are often present near anchorages.
Costa Rica rewards those who pay attention to their surroundings.
whyCharter: Gulf of Papagayo — protected bay, established infrastructure, reliable dry season conditions
Humpback whales — seasonal migration along the Pacific coast
Cocos Island — remote, biodiverse, expedition-led extension
Nicoya Peninsula — less visited coastline with surf and remote anchorages
Wildlife throughout — marine and coastal ecosystems in close proximity
A nature-led charter experience distinct from traditional cruising grounds

locations.name: Galápagos Islands
locations.tagline: Expedition-led itineraries shaped by wildlife found nowhere else
description: The Galápagos Islands are unlike any charter destination — and the regulations that govern them are central to what defines the experience.

Access is strictly controlled by the Ecuadorian government. Charter vessels must be licensed, itineraries are pre-approved, and visitor numbers at each site are limited. This is not a constraint — it is what has preserved an archipelago that Darwin described as a living laboratory, and what ensures wildlife encounters remain consistent and protected.

The wildlife here shows little fear of humans. Giant tortoises, marine iguanas, blue-footed boobies, Galápagos sea lions and flightless cormorants continue their natural behaviour in close proximity to visitors. Underwater, hammerhead sharks, whale sharks, manta rays and sea turtles are encountered regularly. The density and variety of species — many endemic — is the reason clients come.
Puerto Ayora on Santa Cruz is the primary base. Itineraries move between islands along approved routes, with each location offering a distinct ecosystem.
A Galápagos charter requires specialist planning and advance booking. The experience justifies both.
locations.footer: The Galápagos rewards patience and curiosity. Few destinations offer this level of consistency and proximity to wildlife.
whyCharter: Endemic wildlife — giant tortoises, marine iguanas, blue-footed boobies
Underwater encounters — hammerheads, whale sharks, manta rays, sea turtles
Strictly regulated — preserving consistent wildlife experiences
Each island offers a distinct ecosystem
Year-round destination — seasonal variation shapes encounters
One of the most significant natural environments in the world

locations.name: Brazil
locations.tagline: Fernando de Noronha, the Amazon, and an emerging charter destination of exceptional range
description: Brazil is an emerging charter destination — vast, biodiverse and still developing the infrastructure that more established regions take for granted. For those prepared to plan carefully with specialist operators, the rewards are significant.

Fernando de Noronha is the most compelling coastal proposition. This UNESCO World Heritage archipelago, approximately 350 kilometres off the northeast coast, operates under strict visitor controls — a daily environmental tax, limited access and no large-scale tourism. The water is exceptionally clear, spinner dolphins are frequently present, and the level of preservation is among the highest in the South Atlantic. Charter options are limited and specialist — advance planning with the right operator is essential.

The Amazon offers a completely different experience. River vessels navigate one of the most biodiverse environments in the world — pink river dolphins, caimans, extensive birdlife and a scale of landscape that is difficult to anticipate. Manaus is the primary gateway. These are specialist itineraries operated by experienced local operators, and they are not directly comparable to conventional charter.
Brazil rewards those who approach it with patience and the right guidance. It is not a destination for the unprepared — but for those who engage with it properly, it is highly rewarding.
whyCharter: Fernando de Noronha — UNESCO World Heritage, clear water, protected access
Strict visitor controls — high levels of environmental preservation
Amazon river charters — pink dolphins, caimans, exceptional biodiversity
Specialist local operators with deep regional knowledge
Limited access — a defining part of the experience

name: Indian Ocean
tagline: Turquoise atolls, granite islands and some of the finest diving in the world
intro: The Indian Ocean is one of the most naturally distinctive charter regions — and one that rewards a more considered approach.

The Maldives, the Seychelles and Mauritius each offer a different expression of the region. Shallow turquoise atolls, granite islands rising from deep water, and coral reef systems of exceptional biodiversity define the landscape. The diving — particularly in the Maldives — ranks among the finest available globally.

The fleet is more limited than in the Mediterranean or Caribbean, and planning is correspondingly more important. The Maldives has the most established local charter fleet, offering strong regional experience and access to the atolls. In the Seychelles, a smaller number of yachts operate across both the inner and outer islands, with the latter requiring more time and careful planning. Mauritius is less defined by cruising alone, but offers a well-positioned base with strong shoreside depth.
The season runs from November to April ahead of the southwest monsoon. Early booking is essential, particularly in the Seychelles where availability can be limited.
The Indian Ocean rewards patience. The destination consistently justifies it.

locations.name: The Maldives
locations.tagline: Atolls, exceptional diving and a destination that operates on two entirely different seasons
description: The Maldives is one of the few charter destinations that genuinely functions year-round — though the experience changes completely depending on when you arrive.

From November to April, the northeast monsoon brings calm seas and exceptional visibility. The atolls — North and South Malé, Baa and Ari — offer some of the finest diving in the world. Manta rays, whale sharks and reef systems of remarkable biodiversity define the experience, supported by a well-established local fleet with strong regional knowledge.

From May to October, the southwest monsoon brings swell — and with it, a very different charter. The south atolls, particularly Huvadhoo and the Gaafu groups, offer some of the most consistent and uncrowded surf breaks globally. This is liveaboard territory, where itineraries are built around conditions and access to remote reef passes.

One of the Maldives' defining advantages is regulatory. Charter vessels are often licensed to carry more than twelve guests — allowing larger groups to travel together in a way that is rarely possible in the Mediterranean or Caribbean.
The Maldives rewards those who understand when to go — and what they want from it.
whyCharter: Dual-season destination — diving and surfing at different times of year
Exceptional diving — manta rays, whale sharks, high biodiversity
South atolls — consistent, uncrowded surf breaks
Larger group capacity — vessels often licensed beyond twelve guests
Well-established local fleet with strong regional expertise
A destination defined by water, space and flexibility

locations.name: The Seychelles
locations.tagline: Granite islands, deep water and one of the most visually distinctive cruising grounds in the world
description: The Seychelles offer a charter experience defined by contrast — granite islands rising sharply from deep blue water, dense vegetation running to the shoreline, and anchorages that feel both dramatic and protected.

Mahé is the natural starting point, with access to Praslin and La Digue within a short passage. This inner island group forms the core of most charters — manageable distances, reliable conditions and a concentration of some of the most recognisable landscapes in the Indian Ocean. Beaches such as Anse Source d'Argent are as striking from the water as they are ashore, and the cruising between islands is as much a part of the experience as the destinations themselves.

Beyond this, the outer islands introduce a more remote character. Aldabra and the far reaches of the archipelago are accessible only with time, range and careful planning — a different category of charter entirely, but one that rewards those who commit to it.
The fleet is limited, and availability can be tight in peak season. Those who plan early find one of the most complete sailing environments in the Indian Ocean.
whyCharter: Granite island landscape — visually unique within the Indian Ocean
Inner islands — ideal distances and consistent cruising conditions
Anse Source d'Argent — one of the most recognisable beaches globally
Outer islands — remote, lightly visited and expedition-level access
Clear, deep water and strong sailing environment
A natural balance between accessibility and remoteness

locations.name: Mauritius
locations.tagline: Volcanic landscape, reef-protected lagoons and a more private expression of the Indian Ocean
description: Mauritius offers a different kind of charter experience — less defined by extensive cruising, more by the combination of sea, landscape and refined shoreside life.

The island is encircled by coral reef, creating sheltered lagoons along much of the coastline. Le Morne, on the southwest tip, is the defining landscape — a UNESCO-listed mountain rising above clear, shallow water, with kitesurfers and yachts sharing the same horizon. The east coast offers a series of protected anchorages and access to Île aux Cerfs, while the north around Grand Baie provides the most developed marina infrastructure and provisioning.

Mauritius is not a high-volume charter market. A very limited number of yachts operate here, alongside a small selection of well-managed local vessels. Availability is tight, and most charters require early planning or access to privately positioned yachts in the region.

What Mauritius offers instead is control and discretion — a destination where time is split easily between water and shore. World-class resorts, golf, and a cultural mix of Indian, French and Creole influence give it a depth that extends beyond the coastline.
For those who approach it with the right expectations, Mauritius delivers a quieter, more private version of the Indian Ocean.
whyCharter: Limited fleet — access-driven and inherently exclusive
Reef-protected lagoons — calm, sheltered cruising
Le Morne — one of the most striking landscapes in the Indian Ocean
Strong shoreside offering — resorts, golf and cultural depth
A natural complement to Seychelles or South Africa itineraries
A more private, less trafficked charter environment

name: Arabian Gulf & Red Sea
tagline: Winter sun, exceptional diving, and a distinctly different charter experience
intro: The Arabian Gulf and Red Sea offer a charter experience entirely distinct from the Mediterranean or Caribbean — different light, different culture, and a pace shaped as much by place as by season.

The Gulf has developed rapidly as a charter destination. Dubai is the headline — a city defined by scale, with world-class marina infrastructure and some of the most ambitious hospitality in the world. Abu Dhabi offers a more considered counterpart, with cultural depth and a quieter expression of the same standard. Oman, particularly the Musandam Peninsula, provides something the UAE cannot — dramatic fjord-like inlets, near-total quiet, and a landscape that feels entirely removed from the developments to the north.

The Red Sea is one of the world's most established diving regions. The coral reefs along the Egyptian coast — among the most biodiverse in the region — support a specialist charter fleet operating from Hurghada and Sharm el-Sheikh. The water is warm, clear, and well suited to itineraries built around diving and snorkelling.
The charter season runs from October to April across both regions — winter sun at its most accessible.

seasonConditions.charterBases: Dubai · Abu Dhabi · Muscat · Hurghada · Sharm el-Sheikh

locations.name: Dubai & the UAE
locations.tagline: World-class marina infrastructure, ambitious hospitality, and a contemporary charter environment
description: Dubai is unlike any other charter destination — and that is precisely what makes it worth experiencing.

The city is the itinerary. Cruising past the Burj Al Arab, anchoring off the Palm Jumeirah, watching the Dubai Fountain from the water at dusk — Dubai delivers a charter experience that no traditional cruising ground can replicate. It is urban, ambitious, and executed to a standard that reflects a city built on scale and intent.

Dubai Marina is the charter base — one of the most developed marina environments in the world, surrounded by restaurants, beach clubs and waterfront infrastructure that makes every aspect of the charter seamless. The fleet is predominantly motor yachts, well suited to a destination where the experience is shaped by what you see rather than how far you travel.

Abu Dhabi, ninety minutes up the coast, offers a natural extension. The Louvre Abu Dhabi seen from the water is one of the more distinctive architectural moments in the region. Sir Bani Yas Island, a wildlife reserve accessible by sea, adds a different dimension to what might otherwise be a purely urban itinerary.
Between the two cities, the Arabian Gulf charter experience is complete.
whyCharter: Dubai Marina — one of the most developed charter bases globally
The city as the destination — Burj Al Arab, Palm Jumeirah, Dubai Fountain
World-class restaurants, beach clubs and hospitality directly on the waterfront
Abu Dhabi — Louvre, Sir Bani Yas Island, Formula One circuit
Predominantly motor yacht fleet — well suited to the cruising environment
Winter sun at its most consistent and accessible

locations.name: Oman
locations.tagline: The Musandam Peninsula, the khors, and a quieter expression of the Arabian Gulf
description: Oman is the quieter, more natural counterpart to the UAE — and for those who find it, often the more memorable of the two.

The Musandam Peninsula is the defining experience. Known as the Norway of Arabia, its khors — dramatic fjord-like inlets cut into limestone mountains — are largely inaccessible except by sea. The water is clear, the cliffs are vertical, and dolphins are frequently present. Khasab is the base, a small town at the northern tip that feels entirely removed from the development of the cities to the south.

Muscat, the capital, offers a completely different character. The city has preserved its architecture and pace with unusual care — the Grand Mosque, the old corniche, the Sultan's Palace seen from the water. It is one of the more elegant capitals in the region and rewards those who arrive by sea.

Bandar Khayran, south of Muscat, is well known to those familiar with Oman — quiet anchorages, sea turtles, excellent snorkelling and a sense of having found somewhere that remains largely overlooked.
Oman's hospitality is genuine and unhurried. The landscape is ancient. The charter experience here is something the Gulf's more developed destinations cannot easily replicate.
whyCharter: Musandam Peninsula — the Norway of Arabia, khors accessible primarily by sea
Dolphins — regularly encountered throughout the Musandam
Muscat — one of the more elegant capitals in the region
Bandar Khayran — sea turtles, quiet anchorages, largely overlooked
Genuine hospitality and an ancient landscape
A quieter, more natural expression of the Gulf charter experience

locations.name: The Red Sea
locations.tagline: Egypt's coral coast. One of the most established diving regions in the world
description: The Red Sea is, first and foremost, a diving destination. The coral reefs along the Egyptian coast are among the most biodiverse and best preserved in the region — warm, clear water, strong visibility, and a marine ecosystem that attracts specialist charter clients globally.

Hurghada is the primary charter base on the northern coast — well connected, well equipped, with access to the offshore reef systems that define the region. Sharm el-Sheikh, at the southern tip of the Sinai Peninsula, sits alongside Ras Mohammed National Park — one of the most recognised dive sites in the world, where reef walls drop into deep water and marine life is abundant.

Further offshore, The Brothers Islands, Elphinstone and Daedalus Reef offer some of the most consistent big-fish diving in the region. Hammerhead sharks, oceanic whitetips and manta rays are regularly encountered. The Thistlegorm wreck — one of the most established dive sites in the world — lies within reach of both bases.
The Red Sea's liveaboard charter tradition is well established. Purpose-built diving vessels combine comfortable accommodation with access to remote reefs that day boats cannot reach.
For itineraries shaped by what lies beneath the surface, the Red Sea remains in a category of its own.
whyCharter: Ras Mohammed — one of the most recognised dive sites globally
The Brothers Islands & Elphinstone — consistent big-fish diving
Thistlegorm wreck — one of the most established wreck dives in the world
Warm, clear water year-round with strong visibility
Established liveaboard fleet — access to remote reef systems
A specialist charter destination built around the underwater environment

name: South East Asia
tagline: Ancient waters, exceptional biodiversity, and a region defined by range
intro: South East Asia is one of the most varied charter regions in the world — a collection of cruising grounds that differ as much from each other as they do from the Mediterranean or Caribbean.

The region spans some of the most biodiverse marine environments globally. Indonesia's Raja Ampat, Thailand's Andaman Sea and Malaysia's Langkawi archipelago together offer an unusual breadth of experience — from limestone karsts and sheltered bays to remote island chains and open water. Infrastructure varies accordingly, from the established facilities of Singapore and Phuket to the more remote waters of eastern Indonesia.

Singapore sits at the centre of the region — a natural gateway and operational base — while the surrounding cruising grounds define the experience. Thailand offers the most accessible charter environment, Indonesia the greatest sense of scale and remoteness, and Malaysia a quieter, well-protected alternative.

The charter season varies by territory. Thailand and the Andaman Sea are best from November to April. Indonesia operates across much of the year, with seasonal movement between regions. Singapore functions year-round.
South East Asia rewards those who plan carefully. The further you move beyond the familiar, the more it offers.

locations.name: Singapore
locations.tagline: The gateway to South East Asia and one of the region's leading maritime hubs
description: Singapore is the natural starting point for charter in South East Asia — a city where infrastructure, access and service operate at a consistently high standard.

ONE°15 Marina Sentosa Cove is the primary base — a well-established superyacht facility with direct access to the city, strong provisioning and a level of efficiency that makes embarkation straightforward. From the water, the approach to Marina Bay — the skyline, Gardens by the Bay and the density of the city — provides a distinctive arrival.

Ashore, Singapore offers one of the most refined urban experiences in Asia. The food scene is exceptional, from local hawker centres to Michelin-starred restaurants, and the cultural mix reflects its position between Chinese, Malay, Indian and Western influences. It is safe, efficient and easy to navigate — a practical advantage for both short stays and charter transitions.
Singapore is less about extended cruising and more about positioning — a base from which Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia are all within reach.
whyCharter: ONE°15 Marina — established superyacht base with strong infrastructure
Marina Bay — distinctive urban arrival from the water
Gateway to Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia
Exceptional food scene across all levels
Reliable, year-round conditions
A practical and efficient starting point for regional charters

locations.name: Indonesia
locations.tagline: Bali, Komodo and Raja Ampat. One of the most biodiverse marine regions in the world
description: Indonesia is a different proposition entirely. Spread across over 17,000 islands, it offers one of the richest marine environments on earth, and a scale of landscape that sets it apart from more established charter regions.

Bali is the natural entry point — a charter base with established facilities at Benoa Harbour, significant cultural depth ashore, and access to Nusa Penida, where manta rays gather regularly at cleaning stations.

The passage east opens up the archipelago. Lombok and the Gili Islands provide a first extension — quieter, less visited, with strong reef systems. Komodo comes next — the dragons are the headline, but the diving, pink sand beaches and volcanic landscape define the experience.

Raja Ampat is the furthest reach and the defining reward. Limestone islands rise from calm water in near-abstract formations, and beneath the surface, marine biodiversity is among the highest recorded globally. This is liveaboard territory, requiring expedition-level planning and time to do properly.
Indonesia rewards commitment. The further east you go, the more it reveals.
whyCharter: Raja Ampat — among the most biodiverse marine environments globally
Nusa Penida — consistent manta ray encounters
Komodo — unique wildlife and dramatic landscapes
Bali — cultural depth with established charter infrastructure

locations.name: Thailand
locations.tagline: The Andaman Sea, Phang Nga Bay and the Similan Islands
description: Thailand is the most established and accessible charter destination in South East Asia — and for many clients, the natural introduction to the region.

Phuket is the primary base. Royal Phuket Marina and Yacht Haven provide well-established superyacht facilities, strong provisioning and direct international access. Most seven-day charters head north into Phang Nga Bay.

Phang Nga Bay is the defining experience. Limestone karsts rise vertically from calm, green water — some hollow, others concealing hidden lagoons accessible only by tender. The light in early morning and late afternoon, and the scale of the bay, set it apart from more familiar cruising grounds. James Bond Island sits within the bay, though it is the surrounding anchorages that define the experience.
Ko Phi Phi, to the south, is reachable on a standard charter — steep cliff walls, clear water and some of the most recognisable scenery in Thailand.

Those with more time are rewarded further afield. The Similan Islands offer exceptional diving and near-total quiet but require ten days or more to reach comfortably. Ko Lipe, close to the Malaysian border, is similarly suited to longer itineraries.
Thai hospitality, aboard and ashore, is a defining part of the experience.
whyCharter: Phang Nga Bay — limestone karsts, hidden lagoons, distinctive light
Ko Phi Phi — accessible within a standard seven-day charter
Similan Islands — exceptional diving, suited to longer itineraries
Phuket — established base with strong infrastructure
Thai hospitality — consistently high standard aboard and ashore
