locations.name: Malaysia
locations.tagline: Langkawi — a protected archipelago with established charter infrastructure
description: Langkawi sits at the northwest tip of Malaysia — an archipelago of around 100 islands, with sheltered waters and reliable conditions for much of the year.

The Langkawi International Yacht Registry and the marinas at Telaga Harbour and the Royal Langkawi Yacht Club provide solid infrastructure — making it a practical base for yachts moving between Thailand and Singapore.

As a charter destination, Langkawi is quieter and more contained than neighbouring cruising grounds. The islands offer sheltered anchorages, mangrove channels and limestone karst scenery, with a pace that encourages a more relaxed itinerary. The Kilim Karst Geoforest Park — Asia's first UNESCO Geopark — is accessible by sea, and duty-free status simplifies provisioning.
Langkawi is best understood as part of a wider regional itinerary — a place to pause between Thailand and Singapore, with enough natural appeal and infrastructure to justify time in its own right.
Penang, to the south, adds a further dimension — a multicultural island with colonial heritage and one of the strongest food scenes in the region.
whyCharter: Langkawi — sheltered waters, duty-free provisioning, established infrastructure
Kilim Karst Geoforest Park — UNESCO-listed, accessible by sea
Natural link between Thailand and Singapore
Mangrove channels and protected anchorages throughout
Penang — colonial heritage and a standout regional food scene
A quieter alternative to more established cruising grounds

name: South Pacific
tagline: Reef lagoons, volcanic peaks and some of the most remote cruising on earth
intro: The South Pacific is one of the most visually distinctive charter regions in the world — and one of the most geographically remote.

French Polynesia, Fiji and Tonga together form a cruising ground of exceptional range. Each is defined by its own character, landscape and relationship with the sea. What connects them is the quality of the water, the consistency of the conditions and a sense of remoteness that is increasingly difficult to find elsewhere.

French Polynesia sits at the centre of the region — Bora Bora, the Society Islands and the Tuamotu Atolls forming a cruising ground as refined as it is distinctive. Fiji offers a different proposition: a well-established charter fleet, exceptional diving and an archipelago of over 300 islands, supported by solid infrastructure and genuine warmth. Tonga lies further east — remote, lightly visited and defined by one of the most remarkable wildlife encounters in the Pacific, as humpback whales migrate through the Vava'u group between July and October.
The charter season runs broadly from May to November, outside the cyclone period. Distances between island groups are significant, and itineraries are built around time, wind and range.
This is a region that rewards commitment. The further you travel, the more it offers.

locations.name: Fiji
locations.tagline: Island chains, reef systems and a cruising ground defined by variety rather than uniformity
description: Fiji offers a broader, less structured charter experience than French Polynesia — a destination where the appeal lies in the range of its cruising rather than a single defining landscape.

The Mamanuca and Yasawa Islands form the core of most itineraries. Located to the west of Viti Levu, these island groups provide the most accessible cruising — reef-protected waters, consistent conditions and a balance between developed anchorages and quieter bays. Distances are manageable and well suited to a standard charter.

The character shifts further afield. The Yasawas become more remote toward the north — fewer resorts, more open anchorages and a stronger sense of separation from the mainland. Reef systems throughout offer clear water and strong diving, with coral health and marine life varying noticeably between locations.

Fiji's charter fleet is developing rather than established. A small number of well-managed yachts operate here, supported by locally based vessels with strong regional knowledge. Availability is limited, and itineraries often require flexibility.

What Fiji offers is contrast — between islands, between anchorages, and between the accessible and the remote. It is a destination that benefits from a considered approach, and rewards those who allow the itinerary to evolve as they move through it.
whyCharter: Mamanuca Islands — accessible, reef-protected cruising close to base
Yasawa Islands — increasingly remote and less developed to the north
Varied anchorages — from resort-backed bays to quieter open water
Strong snorkelling and diving across multiple reef systems
Developing charter fleet — limited, but improving
A destination defined by contrast rather than repetition

locations.name: French Polynesia
locations.tagline: Bora Bora, reef lagoons and one of the most visually distinctive charter destinations in the world
description: French Polynesia is the centre of South Pacific charter — a destination where the landscape is as defining as the cruising itself.

The Society Islands form the core. Tahiti is the gateway, but it is Raiatea and Taha'a that establish the rhythm — shared lagoon cruising, short passages and anchorages set between reef edge and sheltered interior. Bora Bora sits at the southern edge, its lagoon and volcanic peak forming one of the most recognisable anchorages in the world. Approached by sea, it remains as striking as its reputation suggests.

Moorea, just northwest of Tahiti, offers immediate contrast — steep green peaks rising directly from the water, deep bays and a sense of scale that feels closer and more dramatic than the outer islands.
The cruising is defined by the reef. Lagoons provide protected water and extraordinary clarity, while passes introduce a more technical element when moving between island groups.

Further afield, the Tuamotu Atolls offer a different experience — low-lying coral formations, narrow passes and some of the most advanced diving in the Pacific, best suited to yachts with the range to reach them.
French Polynesia is not about variety in the Mediterranean sense. It is about refinement — a single landscape explored properly.
whyCharter: Bora Bora — one of the most recognisable lagoon anchorages in the world
Society Islands — structured cruising with short, well-balanced passages
Reef-protected lagoons — calm water and exceptional clarity throughout
Moorea — dramatic topography within immediate reach of Tahiti
Tuamotu Atolls — remote, technically rewarding diving and cruising
A visually defined destination — consistent, distinctive and unmistakable

locations.name: Tonga
locations.tagline: Remote anchorages, clear water and one of the few places in the world where you can swim with whales
description: Tonga is one of the most specialised charter destinations in the South Pacific — a place defined not by infrastructure or scale, but by a single, extraordinary natural encounter.

The Vava'u island group forms the centre of charter activity. A protected network of islands, deep anchorages and short passages, it offers calm, clear cruising in a setting that feels largely unchanged. The landscape is less dramatic than French Polynesia, but the water — and what moves through it — defines the experience.

From July to October, humpback whales migrate to these waters to breed and calve. Tonga is one of the few places in the world where regulated in-water encounters are permitted. For many clients, this is the reason to come — and the reason itineraries are built almost entirely around the whales.

Outside this period, the cruising is quiet and lightly visited. Anchorages are simple, distances manageable, and the pace unhurried. Infrastructure is limited, and the fleet typically consists of smaller expedition yachts or locally based vessels with strong regional knowledge.
Tonga does not offer variety in the conventional sense. It offers focus — a charter shaped around a moment that very few places in the world can provide.
whyCharter: Humpback whales — one of the only places globally for regulated in-water encounters
Vava'u — protected island group with calm, accessible cruising
Low charter density — quiet, lightly visited and highly selective
Clear water — excellent visibility throughout the season
A highly focused experience — built around wildlife rather than itinerary
A destination that cannot be replicated elsewhere

name: Australia & New Zealand
tagline: Great Barrier Reef, open coastlines and a charter region defined by scale, access and intent
intro: Australia and New Zealand offer a charter experience defined by quality rather than density — a region where the right yacht, the right timing and the right itinerary deliver something genuinely exceptional.

The Whitsundays and the Great Barrier Reef form the core of Australian charter. Protected waters, consistent conditions and a natural island chain make the region well suited to multi-day itineraries, with Hamilton Island and Airlie Beach as the primary bases.

Sydney operates differently — one of the world's great harbour cities and a major centre for event and static charters. Demand is calendar-driven: New Year's Eve, major sporting events and private functions. For those willing to extend beyond the harbour, longer itineraries north toward Pittwater are possible.

New Zealand introduces a more conditional charter environment. Auckland is the principal gateway, with the Bay of Islands offering the most practical cruising ground — sheltered, wildlife-rich and well suited to a considered itinerary. Beyond this, charter activity depends largely on repositioning yachts and extended programmes.
The season runs from November to April, aligning with the southern hemisphere summer.
A region that rewards planning — and, for those who approach it correctly, delivers something few others can.

seasonConditions.charterBases: Airlie Beach · Hamilton Island · Sydney · Auckland

locations.name: Australia
locations.tagline: Whitehaven Beach, reef passages and one of the most naturally protected cruising grounds in the southern hemisphere
description: The Whitsundays are where Australian charter works best — a compact island chain set within the protection of the Great Barrier Reef, where distances are short, anchorages are reliable and the pace of the itinerary feels naturally balanced.

Hamilton Island and Airlie Beach serve as the primary gateways. From here, the cruising ground opens quickly — Hook Island, Hayman Island and the outer reef systems all within reach of a standard charter. The quality of anchorage defines the experience: calm water, consistent holding and a sense of space that is increasingly rare in more congested regions.

Whitehaven Beach remains the standout. The silica sand shifts with the tide, creating patterns that change throughout the day, and the anchorage off Tongue Bay is one of the most recognisable in Australia. Early mornings and late afternoons are when the landscape is at its best.
The outer reef introduces a different rhythm — reef passages and snorkelling that move from protected lagoon to open coral wall within the same itinerary.
Sydney sits outside this cruising ground but remains commercially relevant — a global harbour used primarily for event and static charters.
Australia rewards a measured approach. Done properly, it is simple, spacious and quietly exceptional.
whyCharter: Protected cruising — reef shelter creates consistently calm conditions
Whitehaven Beach — one of the most distinctive landscapes in Australia
Strong anchorage quality — reliable, well-spaced and uncrowded
Access to outer reef systems — varied snorkelling and diving within one itinerary
Low traffic — a noticeably quieter experience than the Mediterranean
Sydney Harbour — globally recognised setting for event-led charters

locations.name: New Zealand
locations.tagline: Sheltered cruising, long passages and a destination shaped by timing rather than volume
description: New Zealand is a charter destination defined by availability. It is not driven by fleet density or established routes, but by the presence of the right yacht — and the willingness to build an itinerary around it.

Auckland is the natural starting point — a serious yachting city with the infrastructure and technical depth to support larger vessels. From here, the Bay of Islands provides the most coherent cruising ground. Over 140 islands form a sheltered network of anchorages, where movement between them is as much a part of the experience as the stops themselves.

Distance shapes the charter. Reaching the Bay of Islands is a passage, and itineraries tend to favour a slower rhythm — fewer locations, more time at anchor, and a sense of progression that feels deliberate rather than compressed. Wildlife is a constant presence, from dolphins to seabirds, with seasonal migrations adding another layer.

Beyond the north, New Zealand opens into something far less structured. More remote coastlines and southern cruising grounds are accessible, but typically only to privately positioned or repositioning yachts, and with the time to justify the distance.
New Zealand rewards flexibility. The best charters here are not selected — they are assembled.
whyCharter: Bay of Islands — extensive, sheltered cruising across a large island network
Auckland — one of the southern hemisphere's key yachting centres
Wildlife — dolphins, seabirds and seasonal migration throughout
Low charter density — access-led and inherently selective
A slower, more deliberate pace — fewer stops, more time in place
A destination shaped by opportunity rather than fixed itinerary

name: North America
tagline: Old-world summering, expedition wilderness and a charter market defined by intent rather than continuity
intro: North America is not a single cruising ground, but a collection of distinct, highly seasonal destinations — each with its own character, pace and purpose.

New England defines the summer season. From Newport to Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard, the coastline becomes one of the most established yachting circuits in the United States — understated, elegant and shaped as much by time ashore as time on the water. The anchorages are well known, and the rhythm is social: beach clubs, private houses, long lunches and a calendar that reflects a more traditional kind of wealth.

Florida operates in a different capacity — Miami and Fort Lauderdale are among the most important yachting centres in the world, primarily as event bases, departure points for the Bahamas and Caribbean, and staging grounds for the major yacht shows.

Alaska sits at the opposite end of the spectrum. Vast, remote and largely untouched, it offers one of the most compelling expedition charter environments in the Northern Hemisphere. Glaciers, wildlife and protected waterways shape the experience, with itineraries built around distance, conditions and access.
This is a region that rewards clarity. Each destination serves a different purpose — and when chosen correctly, each delivers exactly what it should.

locations.name: New England & New York
locations.tagline: Nantucket, Martha's Vineyard and a summer season defined by tradition, discretion and time well spent
description: New England and New York together form one of the most established summer yachting circuits in the United States — understated, elegant and shaped as much by time ashore as time on the water.

The coastline from Newport to Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard forms the core. Distances are short, the waters are protected, and the experience is defined by arriving well rather than sailing far. Edgartown and Nantucket Town offer some of the most picturesque harbours on the East Coast — weathered shingle houses, strong restaurants and a sense of place that feels preserved rather than constructed.

Further west, the Hamptons and Montauk bring a faster pace — beach clubs, private houses and a weekend energy that draws New York out to the water. Newport, with its sailing heritage and historic estates, remains the natural starting point for most itineraries.
This is a short-season destination that rewards timing. July and August bring the full rhythm of the East Coast summer — regattas, events and a social calendar that quietly defines the experience.
New England and New York do not compete with the Mediterranean. They offer something entirely different — more contained, more discreet, and, for many clients, more personal.
whyCharter: Nantucket & Martha's Vineyard — iconic East Coast summer destinations
Short cruising distances — ideal for relaxed, unhurried itineraries
Newport — historic sailing capital with strong charter infrastructure
The Hamptons & Montauk — beach clubs, private houses, New York's summer escape
Refined, understated atmosphere — distinct from Mediterranean charter

locations.name: Alaska
locations.tagline: Glaciers, wildlife and one of the most compelling expedition charter environments in the Northern Hemisphere
description: Alaska is where North American charter moves into a different category entirely — a destination defined by scale, distance and environment rather than infrastructure or itinerary.

The Inside Passage forms the backbone of most charters — a protected network of channels, fjords and anchorages from Ketchikan to Juneau and Sitka, running through largely untouched landscape. The experience is shaped by movement through wilderness rather than between destinations.

Glacier Bay National Park is the defining highlight. Tidewater glaciers descend into the sea, calving ice at a scale that is difficult to anticipate. Access is permit-controlled — a reflection of the environment's sensitivity.
Wildlife is a constant presence — humpback whales, orcas, bears along remote shorelines, bald eagles and sea lions — creating a landscape that feels active without ever feeling crowded.

This is not a destination for conventional itineraries. Distances, weather and light shape each charter, and the best programmes remain flexible — allowing time to follow wildlife, adjust to conditions and fully engage with the scale of what surrounds you.
The fleet is limited, with expedition yachts and experienced crews.
Alaska is not about arrival. It is about progression — a charter defined by the journey itself, and by a landscape that reveals its scale gradually.
whyCharter: Inside Passage — protected, extended cruising through wilderness
Glacier Bay — one of the most dramatic glacier environments in the world
Wildlife — whales, bears, orcas and eagles throughout the region
Expedition cruising — serious, remote and experience-led
Low charter density — vast, uncrowded and largely untouched
A Northern Hemisphere counterpart to Norway and Greenland

name: Antarctica
tagline: Ice, silence and the furthest reach of the charter world
intro: Antarctica is not a destination in the conventional sense. It is the point at which the idea of travel changes entirely — where infrastructure disappears, itineraries dissolve, and the experience becomes defined by environment rather than intention.

For most clients, the journey begins long before arrival. Ushuaia, at the southern tip of Argentina, is the last recognisable port before the crossing south. Beyond it lies the Drake Passage — a stretch of open water that has, for centuries, marked the boundary between the inhabited world and something far more remote. Two days later, conditions permitting, the first ice appears.
From here, everything slows.

locations.name: Antarctica
locations.tagline: Crossing the Drake to penguins, whales, and ice that never stops moving

sections.heading: The Reality of Chartering Antarctica
body: Antarctica is one of the most complex and restricted environments on earth. Access is governed under the Antarctic Treaty System, with strict environmental controls that dictate how vessels operate, where landings can be made, and how many people can go ashore at any one time.
There is no meaningful charter fleet in the traditional sense.

At the private level, only a small number of ice-strengthened expedition yachts globally are capable of operating safely in these waters. These are not standard superyachts — they are purpose-built vessels, equipped for polar navigation and crewed by teams with genuine expedition experience. Availability is limited, and programmes are typically planned many months, if not years, in advance.

Alongside this, a separate category exists: expedition cruise vessels. These offer structured itineraries on a cabin basis, often with strong guiding teams and access to the same landscapes, but without the privacy or flexibility of a fully chartered yacht.
Understanding the distinction is essential. The experience is exceptional in both cases — but fundamentally different.

sections.heading: The Experience
body: The Antarctic Peninsula provides the most accessible entry point into the continent, though "accessible" remains relative. Glaciers descend directly into the sea, icebergs drift in silence, and anchorages are temporary — defined by shelter, light and shifting ice rather than charted harbours.
Movement is dictated by conditions. Wind, visibility and ice density determine each day's plan, and the best itineraries are those that remain deliberately flexible.

Wildlife encounters are constant, but never staged. Penguin colonies occupy exposed shorelines, seals rest on drifting ice, and whales move through feeding grounds with little regard for human presence. Landings are made by tender, often onto ice or remote beaches, with each arrival feeling provisional — part of a landscape that does not adjust to accommodate visitors.
What defines Antarctica is not a single moment, but a cumulative sense of scale and stillness. Sound carries differently. Light behaves differently. Time, for most, begins to feel less structured.

sections.heading: Yachts & Access
body: For those considering Antarctica privately, vessel choice is everything.

True expedition yachts — typically larger, heavily built and ice-capable — allow for a fully bespoke programme, with the flexibility to adapt daily based on conditions. These charters are rare, expensive and logistically complex, but represent the highest level of access available.

Expedition cruise vessels offer a more structured alternative. Larger in scale, they operate fixed itineraries with experienced guides, often delivering exceptional wildlife and landing opportunities within a shared environment.
Both approaches are valid. The decision is less about destination, and more about how you choose to experience it.

locations.footer: Antarctica is not about choice or variety. It is about commitment — to the journey, to the conditions, and to a destination that offers very little compromise. For those who make it there, it rarely compares to anything that comes before or after.
whyCharter: Antarctic Peninsula — the most visually striking and accessible part of the continent
Ice-scale environment — glaciers, icebergs and landscapes on an unmatched scale
Wildlife encounters — penguins, seals and whales in a protected ecosystem
Expedition access — one of the few remaining truly remote travel experiences
Highly regulated — preserving the integrity of the environment
A destination that sits entirely outside conventional charter
